# Sociodemographic Disparities in Exposures to Inorganic Contaminants in United States Public Water Systems

**Authors:** Mona Q. Dai; Xindi C. Hu; Brent A. Coull; Chris Campbell; David Q. Andrews; Olga V. Naidenko; Elsie M. Sunderland

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Environmental and Occupational Health, Milken Institute School of Public Health, George Washington University, Washington, District of Columbia, USA | 3Department of Environmental Health, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 5Environmental Working Group, Washington, District of Columbia, USA

## Abstract

Maximum contaminant level violations occur more frequently among some public water systems (PWS) serving marginalized communities across the United States. Spatially resolved PWS service area data are now available, allowing for better understanding of relationships between sociodemographic factors and water quality.

We examined associations between detection and concentrations of arsenic (As), chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn), and selenium (Se) and the sociodemographic characteristics of residents served by PWS at two spatial scales: PWS service areas and counties.

We leveraged data on inorganic contaminants in $greater than 273000$ drinking water samples from $more than 21000$ PWS collected by state agencies and the US Environmental Protection Agency over the decade between 2005–2015 and curated in a national database developed by the Environmental Working Group. Sociodemographic data were from the 2006–2015 American Community Survey. We developed two-step hurdle models that included: a) a categorical model predicting contaminant detection and b) a continuous model predicting contaminant concentration. We developed these hurdle models using PWS service areas or counties as spatial units of analysis and compared results.

PWS serving 5% higher proportions of limited English–speaking households had significantly greater detections of As, Cr, and Se, ranging from 1.25 [95% confidence interval (CI): 1.18, 1.32] times higher probability of Cr detection to 1.69 (95% CI: 1.58, 1.80) times higher probability of Se detection. Small PWS ( $less than or equal to 10000$ customers) had higher concentrations of these same three contaminants. PWS serving greater proportions of Black residents had a lower probability of detecting As, Cr, and Se, but significantly higher concentrations of Cr, Mn, and Se, particularly outside large urban areas. The direction of significant associations was consistent between spatial units of analysis, but county results tended to exhibit greater effect sizes and fewer significant associations.

PWS service area data help to identify drinking water concerns specific to served communities and reduce issues related to statistical bias at larger spatial scales. Targeted subsidies for water infrastructure in communities served by small PWS would help reduce disparities in exposures to drinking water contaminants. https://doi.org/10.1289/EHP14793

## Introduction

Exposures to inorganic contaminants, such as arsenic (As), chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn), and selenium (Se), commonly detected in drinking water, have been associated with various adverse health effects including diabetes,1 neurotoxicity,2 miscarriage, endocrine disruption, and cancer.3 In the United States, regulations specifying maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) for inorganic toxicants in drinking water from public water systems (PWS) have been in place since the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) was finalized in 1974.4 Since that time, water quality monitoring data have been collected by state and federal agencies as part of the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) for regulated contaminants and the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR) for priority unregulated contaminants.5 These activities have produced a national database on inorganic toxicants that can be mined to better understand differences in exposures to toxicants among sociodemographic groups.5

Past work shows MCL violations are statistically more frequent among PWS serving large proportions of people of color,6,7 populations without health insurance,8 and communities having lower socioeconomic status.7 For example, MCL exceedances for nitrate occurred three times more frequently in community water supplies serving the highest proportion of non-White Hispanic residents in comparison with those serving the lowest proportion of Hispanic residents.9 Similarly, the odds ratio for exceeding the MCL for As was 3.36 [95% confidence interval (CI): 3.03, 3.74] in semiurban Hispanic counties.10 Many drinking water contaminants are still unregulated, and existing MCLs reflect the feasibility of treatment at different levels, costs, and health risks associated with exposure.5 Categorical models are often used to consider disparities relative to existing regulatory thresholds.6–11 However, when research demonstrates substantial risks due to chronic low-level exposures, new MCLs may be established [e.g., per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)],12 and existing standards [e.g., As and lead (Pb)]13,14 have been lowered over time. Thus, information from continuous models would help support new and lowered MCLs.13,14

Prior work on disparities in exposure to drinking water contaminants has mainly used county-level sociodemographic data as the spatial unit of analysis.6–11 More spatially resolved data on PWS service areas are now available, allowing for finer spatial scale analyses of the geographic distributions of drinking water contaminants.15 Modeling assumptions and data analysis methods used to compare national scale sociodemographic and environmental data can affect conclusions regarding potential disparities. The modifiable areal unit problem occurs when outcomes differ depending on the spatial unit of analysis.16 For example, analyses aggregated at large spatial scales may not detect localized patterns relevant to environmental justice questions.17 Most past studies used the county scale spatial unit because precise PWS locations were confidential in many states.6–9,11 Recent availability of PWS service area data15 allows the modifiable areal unit problem to be evaluated for disparities in exposures to drinking water contaminants.

The main objectives of this work were to evaluate a) potential sociodemographic disparities in exposures to three regulated (As, Cr, Se) and one unregulated (Mn) contaminants in drinking water from US PWS and b) how the spatial unit of analysis affects conclusions. We focus on Mn as an unregulated contaminant due to exposure concerns related to neurotoxicity2,18 and good spatial data coverage at the national scale ( $greater than or equal to 75 percent$ of counties represented).19 For each contaminant, we developed novel hurdle models to examine associations between the sociodemographic composition of customers served by PWS and the probability of detecting contaminants and detectable concentrations. We compared results for two spatial units of analysis (PWS service area and county) and stratified analyses across different population density indicators (metropolitan, nonmetropolitan, large PWS, and small PWS).

## Methods

### Data Sources

#### Drinking water data.

We obtained data collected by 49 state agencies and the US Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) (Table S1), mainly as part of compliance with the SDWA,5 curated in a national database developed by the Environmental Working Group (EWG).20 EWG compiled state data repositories that were directly accessible online and requested unavailable data from the responsible state agencies. This work focuses on As ( $lowercase italic n equals 448448$ samples), Cr ( $lowercase italic n equals 279355$ ), Mn ( $lowercase italic n equals 274872$ ), and Se ( $lowercase italic n equals 273678$ ) in finished (post treatment) drinking water samples. We removed negative values and outliers above the 99th concentration percentile ( $approximately 1 percent$ of data). For Mn, the only unregulated contaminant, we included data collected by state agencies and the Third Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 3).21 Multiple quality-control steps were used to ensure accuracy of the database, including external reviews by water agencies and utilities prior to data release.22

We selected measurements of drinking water samples between 2005 and 2015 that included 34,137 PWS across all 50 states. Annual data were available for multiple years for some PWS. After excluding outliers above the 99th percentile, we represented each PWS using one value (the 95th percentile of concentrations over the entire study window), following methods established in past work.23 We selected the upper percentile to maximize values that were above the detection limit and therefore informative for continuous modeling. We conducted a sensitivity analysis using the median and 75th percentile concentrations to better understand the impacts of this choice on modeling results (Table S2 and S3). Drinking water concentration data in all tables and models are in units of micrograms per liter ( $microgram per liter$ ).

#### PWS data.

We downloaded available PWS service area boundaries from an open-source spatial dataset created by SimpleLab ( $lowercase italic n equals 45499$ PWS).15 These boundaries define the residential regions of customers connected to the same drinking water treatment facility. The dataset is based on locations provided directly by state agencies, assignment to city/town boundaries, or a radius around a city centroid.15 We used these service areas for all PWS included in the EWG drinking water contaminant database between 2005 and 2015. Numbers of PWS with both service area boundaries and drinking water data that were included in our study ranged from 21,680 (Mn) to 34,137 (As) (Table 1).

We obtained data on PWS size, age, type, water source (ground water vs. surface water), and state from the US EPA Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS) (Table S1).24 We queried the US EPA web-based application programming interface (API) service for data on all PWS in SDWIS as of January 2021 to maximize the number of PWS included in this study.25 For each PWS during the study window, we recorded water treatment technology use and identified whether a facility ever employed best available technology (BAT)26 for remediating As, Cr, Mn, and Se based on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (Table S4).26

#### Sociodemographic data.

Sociodemographic data and shapefiles (Excel Table S1) were obtained from the National Historical Geographic Information System (NHGIS) based on American Community Survey (ACS) data for the years 2006–2010 and 2011–2015.27 Over 217,000 census block group and 3,000 county TIGER/Line shapefiles were included.27 We averaged values between the two ACS dataset time frames for sociodemographic variables related to race, ethnicity, language, economic status, education, and housing to match the time period of the PWS dataset (Excel Table S2). We used original ACS reporting categories for race and ethnicity (Excel Table S2). We downloaded high-resolution population density raster maps for the most recent year available (2019) from Data For Good to estimate residents living within $30 meter$ grid tiles across the United States.28 By taking into account this information on habitable spaces, we improved our estimates of sociodemographic factors within PWS service areas by using these raster population density data in combination with sociodemographic vector data to perform dasymetric mapping. Dasymetric mapping is the redistribution of quantitative data to more accurately portray data via a continuous surface, rather than artificially imposed boundaries.29

#### Geochemical and environmental data.

We considered well-established geochemical and environmental factors (air temperature, precipitation, and bedrock/aquifer type) from past studies30,31 as predictors in the hurdle models to account for their known influence on the release and mobility of contaminants independently from sociodemographic factors (Excel Table S1). We obtained surface air temperature ( $degrees Celsius$ ) and precipitation (mm) data between 2005 and 2015 at $1 kilometer$ horizontal resolution from a daily surface weather dataset from the Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center (DAAC).32 At both the PWS service area and county spatial units, temperature and precipitation were significantly associated with drinking water contaminants in both steps of the hurdle model (Excel Tables S3 and S4). Bedrock and aquifer types were obtained from a US Geological Survey (USGS) database on principal aquifers.33

Excel Table S1 provides a complete list of predictors that we considered before examining potential sociodemographic disparities. Predictors in Excel Table S1 were only excluded from the final model if they showed strong covariance (Excel Table S3 and S4) with another predictor based on the Spearman rank correlation coefficient (Spearman’s $lowercase rho$ ). If Spearman’s $lowercase rho$ exceeded 0.6 for two variables, we excluded the predictor that was less correlated with inorganic contaminant concentrations to avoid model collinearity.

### Modeling Approach

We developed multiple two-step hurdle models34 for each contaminant (As, Cr, Mn, and Se) to examine associations between sociodemographic factors and inorganic contaminants in drinking water. Hurdle models are commonly used to analyze highly censored (below detection) data because they treat censored and noncensored data separately.35,36 Each of the hurdle models developed for this study leveraged censored and noncensored drinking water data to estimate a probability of detection based on binomial logistic regression modeling. This analysis allowed us to estimate how changes in the sociodemographic composition of PWS service areas and counties affect the probability of detecting drinking water contaminants above the method detection limit (MDL) specified by the SDWA.37

Analytical MDLs for the drinking water data included in this study were prescribed as part of the SDWA requirements but were not reported in the curated dataset.37 We therefore used the highest allowable MDL in the SDWA as a uniform detection threshold for the dataset (Table S5). We replaced values below each contaminant’s highest allowable MDL with zeros. The substitution of low values with zeros does not influence hurdle model results because the first step in the hurdle model categorically predicts whether values are above or below detection.

The second step of the hurdle models employed in this work used only noncensored data to develop a generalized linear regression model. We used this analysis to characterize associations between sociodemographic factors and detectable drinking water contaminant concentrations. We specifically used a gamma error distribution with a log link for the regression models because it provided the best overall fit based on quantile–quantile plot and residual analyses of detectable drinking water contaminants (Figure S1).

### Multiscale Spatial Analysis

We developed hurdle models for each contaminant (As, Cr, Mn, and Se) at two spatial units of analysis (PWS service area and county scales). Two datasets were created by aggregating drinking water and sociodemographic data to either the PWS service area or county scale. After removing duplicate and missing entries, 21,680–34,137 PWS service areas (Table 1) and 2,453–3,093 counties (Table S6) remained in the datasets for analysis.

PWS characteristics, environmental factors, and sociodemographic factors ( $lowercase italic n equals 16$ predictors) were used as predictors in the PWS service area and county models (Excel Table S1). The first and second steps of the hurdle models both used all 16 of these predictors (including using region as a fixed effect) and were set up identically, apart from their respective outcome variables (Equations S1 and S2). The outcome variable for the categorical models was whether a drinking water contaminant (As, Cr, Mn, or Se) was ever detected between 2005 and 2015. The outcome variable for the continuous models was drinking water contaminant concentration among detected samples. We used the same model predictors for the PWS service area and county spatial unit models. No correlations were observed between the sociodemographic and environmental factors except for the proportion of Black residents and temperature (Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0.65$ ) at the county scale (Excel Table S4). Region was included as a fixed effect to control for location-specific differences. All predictors were assumed to be independent in the model except for bedrock type and water source. Bedrock type is mainly important for drinking water sourced from ground water rather than surface water, so we included an interaction term to account for this.38 All continuous predictors were centered and scaled prior to modeling, and significant associations were determined if $lowercase italic p less than 0.05$ . All spatial analyses were conducted in ArcGIS Pro 3.0.1 (Esri) and R (version 4.2.1; R Development Core Team) using the sf package.39

#### County scale.

Prior work has mainly considered sociodemographic disparities in drinking water quality at the county scale because service area data for PWS only recently became available.15 We therefore compared significant results from the PWS service area analysis to those based on the same modeling approach but using county as the spatial unit of analysis.

We aggregated bedrock and precipitation data to the county scale. We assigned a binary code to bedrock types, where “1” represented any overlap with a county and “0” indicated no overlap. We also calculated mean precipitation values by county. States were assigned to a region designated by US Census divisions to be consistent with the sociodemographic data (Table S7).40 To balance the number of counties in each region, we combined the New England and Mid-Atlantic states into one group (Northeast).

Sociodemographic factors at the county scale were reported directly from the US Census40 and did not require transformation. Counties were assigned contaminant concentrations and PWS characteristics based on all overlapping PWS service areas. If multiple PWS served the same county, population-weighted mean values were calculated for continuous predictors and the most frequent value was assigned for dichotomous predictors.

#### PWS service area scale.

Geological and environmental variables, as well as region, were assigned at the PWS service area scale using the same method as in county assignment. PWS characteristics were directly available through SDWIS.24 Sociodemographic information within PWS service areas was calculated using a population-weighting algorithm. #### Sensitivity analysis for population density stratifications.

We stratified hurdle model results by Rural-Urban Continuum Codes (RUCC) $less than or equals to 3$ from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to account for potential differences in population size between metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas (Table S8).41 Metropolitan counties included those in metropolitan areas with population sizes varying from $less than 250000$ to $greater than or equals to 1 million$ .41 Nonmetropolitan counties included the remaining counties.41

We also stratified the models by PWS size. Following definitions established by the US EPA, we classified small PWS as those serving $less than or equals to 10000$ individuals and large PWS as those serving $greater than 10000$ individuals.24 PWS in nonmetropolitan counties and small PWS are not strongly correlated ( $lowercase phi less than or equal to 0.12$ ), indicating the presence of many “small” PWS in metropolitan areas and some large PWS defined as “nonmetropolitan” using RUCC codes (Table S9). Stratified and unstratified models used the same predictors. All statistical models were performed in R (version 4.2.1) using the mgcv and tidyverse packages.42,43

## Results

### Temporal Trends and Detection of Drinking Water Contaminants

Concentrations of As, Cr, Mn, and Se in drinking water were not significantly different across years for the study window between 2005 and 2015 (Figure S2). Correlations between concentrations of each contaminant were weak but statistically significant at the PWS service area scale (Spearman’s $lowercase rho less than or equal to 0.35$ , $lowercase italic p less than 0.01$ ; Excel Table S3), except for Mn with Cr and Se (Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0$ , $lowercase italic p less than 0.3$ ; Excel Table S3). At the county scale, significant moderate correlations were found among As, Cr, and Se (Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0.42 to 0.52$ , $lowercase italic p less than 0.01$ ; Excel Table S4). Mn was weakly significantly correlated with As at the county scale (Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0.19$ , $lowercase italic p less than 0.01$ ; Excel Table S4).

Figure 1 shows the spatial patterns of drinking water concentrations for the four inorganic contaminants included in this study across the United States. Across the study window, 25%–69% of reporting PWS had drinking water with detectable As, Cr, Mn, or Se concentrations at least once between 2005 and 2015 (Table 1). Approximately 184 million Americans were served by PWS with levels of any of the four contaminants above the detection limit. The greatest detection frequency (69%) was observed for the only unregulated contaminant (Mn) considered in this work. Fewer ( $approximately 35 percent$ less) PWS reported Mn concentrations in comparison with the other three contaminants. Lowest As, Cr, and Se concentrations were found in the South Atlantic states, excluding Florida. Mn showed a different spatial pattern than As, Cr, and Se and was lowest in the Mountain region and highest in the West North Central region (especially Minnesota). More generally, Mn concentrations were higher in northern states (Figure 1).

### Incidence of Regulated Contaminant Violations between 2005 and 2015

A relatively low proportion of PWS exceeded health-based drinking water thresholds for As, Cr, and Se over the 2005–2015 period (0%–4% of PWS; Table 1). Highest concentrations were generally observed in Arizona, Texas, and Kansas (in the Southwest and Midwest regions) (Figure 1). The lowest frequency of contaminant detection occurred in the East South Central and South Atlantic regions. For As, we used the updated MCL of $10 micrograms per liter$ established in 200613 for the whole period between 2005 and 2015. A greater proportion of PWS (21%) exceeded the secondary MCL (SMCL) for Mn of $50 micrograms per liter$ . The SMCL for Mn is based on water taste rather than a health protective level, and almost $24 million$ people were served by PWS above this level. An estimated $3.7 million$ people were served by PWS that exceeded the MCL for As at least once between 2005 and 2015. No violations were observed for Cr or Se. After accounting for systems with multiple violations, we estimated $26.6 million$ people were served by PWS that exceeded the SMCL for Mn or MCL for As.

### Associations between Drinking Water Detection and Sociodemographic Composition

#### PWS serving greater numbers of limited English–speaking households.

The first step of the hurdle model developed in this work showed that each PWS service area with a one standard deviation (5%) higher proportion of limited English–speaking households had a greater probability of serving water with detectable As, Cr, and Se. Results ranged from 1.25 (95% CI: 1.18, 1.32) times higher probability of detecting Cr to 1.69 (95% CI: 1.58, 1.80) times higher probability of detecting Se (Table 2). We did not find a significant association between the proportion of limited English–speaking households located within PWS service areas and detection of Mn (Table 2). English proficiency was significantly correlated with the fraction of Hispanic residents (Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0.65$ , $lowercase italic p less than 0.01$ ; Excel Table S3). After running the same models using ethnicity as a predictor instead of limited English–speaking households, each PWS service area with a one standard deviation (5%) higher proportion of Hispanic residents had significantly greater probabilities of detecting As, Cr and Se. Results ranged from 1.26 (95% CI: 1.19, 1.33) times greater for Cr to 1.55 (95% CI: 1.45, 1.64) times greater for Se (Table 2). Thus, we found comparable differences in contaminant detection between PWS serving higher proportions of limited English–speaking households and higher proportion of Hispanic residents (Table 2).

As, Cr, and Se associations remained significant and positive with PWS serving limited English–speaking households when stratifying these PWS between metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas (Table 2). All three contaminant associations also remained significant after stratifying the models by large and small PWS size serving greater than or fewer than 10,000 total customers (Table 2). For small PWS service areas, we found a higher proportion of limited English–speaking households was significantly associated with a lower probability of detecting Mn.

#### PWS serving higher proportions of black residents.

Each PWS service area with a one standard deviation (15%) higher proportion of Black residents was associated with a significantly lower probability of distributing water with detectable regulated contaminants in drinking water. Results ranged from 0.77 (95% CI: 0.71, 0.84) times lower probability of detecting Se to 0.88 (95% CI: 0.82, 0.95) times lower for detecting As (Table 2). No significant association was observed between the proportion of Black residents in PWS service areas and Mn detected in drinking water.

After stratifying between metropolitan and nonmetropolitan PWS, negative associations with drinking water detection remained significant for Se among both stratifications, but only among metropolitan PWS for As and Cr (Table 2). For Mn, a significant negative association was observed for metropolitan PWS, and a significant positive association was observed for nonmetropolitan PWS. When stratifying by PWS size, significant negative associations remained for small facilities for all contaminants except Mn (Table 2).

#### PWS serving higher proportion of residents with $income-to-poverty ratio less than 2$ .

Each PWS with a one standard deviation (15%) higher proportion of residents with income levels below 200% of the federal poverty line [income-to-poverty ratio (PIR) $less than 2$ ] was significantly associated with a 0.80 (95% CI: 0.75, 0.86) times lower probability of serving water with detectable As, 0.87 (95% CI: 0.79, 0.96) times lower probability of detecting Mn, and 0.75 (95% CI: 0.69, 0.82) times lower probability of detecting Se (Table 2). These results imply that PWS serving higher proportions of lower-income residents have a lower probability of serving water with detectable As, Mn, and Se.

After stratifying results between metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas, associations remained significant and negative for As and Se in nonmetropolitan areas only (Table 2). Both associations were attenuated for Mn (Table 2). After stratifying by small and large PWS, associations were only significant among small PWS for As, Mn, and Se (Table 2).

Figure 1 compares national patterns in drinking water contaminants aggregated spatially at the county scale in comparison with the PWS service area scale. Callouts show how drinking water concentrations from PWS service area boundaries within a county can differ across the contiguous US because one county can contain multiple PWS. Callouts in Figure 1 also illustrate how county maps may mask drinking water concentrations at more granular scales because PWS service area boundaries are not continuous.

## Discussion

This study explored sociodemographic disparities in exposure to US drinking water inorganic contaminants based on known injustices rooted in structural racism. The Drinking Water Disparities Framework44 was created to explain how water quality disparities can stem from regulatory failures that neglect how multiple US systems (e.g., housing, infrastructure, health care) reinforce exclusion of minority populations from the intended benefits of regulations.45 As a result of racial discrimination, exposure and health inequities have become unjustifiably normalized.46 These systems have a historic basis45 in de jure segregation practices such as redlining in the 1930s that restricted where people of color and immigrants could afford to live.47 Generations later, these neighborhoods remain largely segregated and still struggle with a lack of resources and services with real ramifications on the built environment, including on water infrastructure and drinking water quality.44 Lack of political representation in these areas often leads to unequal federal enforcement of drinking water standards48 as well as unequal funding for needed maintenance and operation of treatment systems.49,50 Moreover, all individuals have multiple identities (e.g., race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status), and this intersectionality can affect their exposure risk. National models often have difficulty distinguishing intersectional identities of individuals rather than characterizing their relative presence independently due to a lack of data. Below, we present the results of our drinking water exposure models with respect to some of these sociodemographic factors in the context of past US discrimination.

### Summary of Sociodemographic Associations

In this study, PWS service areas with higher proportions of limited English–speaking households were significantly associated with higher detections and concentrations of As, Cr, and Se. Concentrations of Se were significantly higher in metropolitan PWS serving a greater proportion of limited English–speaking households. As, Cr, and Se concentrations were significantly higher among small PWS serving higher proportions of limited English–speaking households. These results are suggestive of a sociodemographic disparity in drinking water exposure to some regulated contaminants (As, Cr, and Se) at the national scale.

In this work, we showed the proportion of limited English–speaking households was correlated with the proportion of Hispanic residents (Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, $lowercase rho equals 0.65$ ). Associations observed in this work thus support the prevailing hypothesis that PWS serving greater proportions of Hispanic residents are exposed to elevated concentrations of drinking water contaminants (Tables 2 and 3).10,23,51 Previous work has shown that Hispanic communities living in unincorporated territories relying on PWS frequently encounter poor drinking water quality.44,52 In some cases, the forced exclusion of these communities from political power has led to a lack of investment in public works projects that could otherwise improve household drinking water quality.44,52 Spanish speakers are not the only potentially marginalized population that may face these challenges. Although we find similar modeling results for limited English–speaking households and Hispanic residents, more than 300 languages are spoken in the United States and fall within the limited English–speaking household subpopulation.53

We found PWS service areas with higher proportions of Black residents had significantly lower detections of As, Cr, and Se. By contrast, we found PWS serving a greater proportion of Black residents were associated with significantly higher concentrations of Cr, Mn, and Se in nonmetropolitan and small PWS. These results indicate lower detections of drinking water contaminants in PWS serving higher proportions of Black residents, but higher relative concentrations of some contaminants when levels are detectable, particularly outside of urban areas and among small PWS service areas. This discrepancy may reflect findings from past work showing selective enforcement of drinking water regulations, including monitoring and reporting requirements, are related to sociodemographic differences among communities.54 Across the United States, more residents identify as non-Hispanic Black in metropolitan areas where PWS serve more diverse communities in comparison with nonmetropolitan regions.55

These results are consistent with past studies that have reported mixed results between proportions of Black residents and drinking water quality. For example, one national study reported higher proportions of Black residents were associated with lower As and uranium concentrations across the United States, except in contaminated regions.51 Another national study showed significantly greater numbers of SDWA violations in low-income communities with higher Black and Hispanic populations.6 Prior work has suggested that the capacity of treatment facilities in urban areas, where most non-Hispanic Black individuals live, can sometimes attenuate national results and lead to a lower probability of detecting contaminants.51 Overall, our results suggest that outside large urban areas, potential disparities in drinking water inorganic contaminant concentrations for Black residents served by small PWS should be further evaluated. This finding is consistent with other work showing very small community water systems have more monitoring and reporting violations than large systems and that rural systems have higher noncompliance rates.56

Our results do not suggest a strong association between lower income as a measure of economic adversity and exposure to drinking water inorganic contaminants at the national scale. We found PWS serving greater proportions of residents with low income ( $income-to-poverty ratio less than 2$ ) were associated with lower detection of As, Mn, and Se, particularly among small PWS. Among small PWS and PWS in nonmetropolitan areas serving greater proportions of low-income residents, concentrations of all three contaminants were consistently lower. This finding for PWS serving higher proportions of low $income-to-poverty ratio less than 2$ individuals may be affected by fluctuations in cost of living across the country that make it difficult to assess socioeconomic challenges. Our results were robust to tests of alternative low-income thresholds such as $income-to-poverty ratio less than 0.5$ and $income-to-poverty ratio less than 1$ (Table S12 and S13). Modeling results suggest that poverty alone, as measured by the ratio between income and the federal poverty level, is not associated with higher drinking water exposure for the inorganic contaminants examined in this work across the United States.

Negative associations between income and drinking water violations have been reported in prior studies.57,58 For example, past work has reported wealthier counties have significantly greater frequencies of MCL violations for US community water systems.58 Greater prevalence of poverty has been associated with lower detection of other drinking water contaminants, such as nitrate and PFAS, at the national scale.9,59 Past work has attributed these results to differences in income levels among urban and rural settings, as well as differences in pollution sources. For example, pollution sources are often more abundant near urban regions where income may be higher.9,59 Among all counties reporting violations, metropolitan counties have been shown to have the highest concentrations of contaminants.60

Our analysis comparing modeling results at the PWS service area and county spatial units of analysis reinforced the idea that considering the modifiable areal unit problem is important for ongoing research on sociodemographic disparities in contaminant exposures. Overall, our results showed similar directionality in the first step of the hurdle models (categorical models) at both spatial units but larger effect sizes at the county scale for detection (Figure 2; Figure S3). For the second step of the hurdle models (continuous models), county scale results showed more limited statistically significant associations in comparison with the PWS service area spatial unit (Figure 3; Figure S4). These differences likely reflect the effect of aggregation bias on variance.16 Consequently, county scale associations appeared to be exaggerated, displaying wider confidence intervals with greater uncertainties. Increased variance due to aggregatin bias likely led to fewer statistically significant associations in the continuous models.

Measuring population characteristics as closely as possible to the community being served best represents how households receiving water are affected by exposure disparities.61 Previous work has primarily focused on county scale analyses, although some state-focused investigations have been conducted at the city or zip code scales.9,62 Counties are more likely to include areas not served by PWS, where private well users reside. Therefore, analyzing sociodemographic disparities at the PWS service area spatial unit likely provides more accurate results.

### Study Strengths and Limitations

Strengths of this study include the use of a large historic dataset covering a decade of samples recorded by almost every state for four inorganic contaminants in public drinking water. Because drinking water is federally regulated, this national analysis can assist in identifying policy-relevant patterns in inequalities across the country. Our analysis highlights that using PWS service areas instead of counties as the spatial unit of analysis may more accurately identify drinking water disparities for populations relying on PWS. This information is essential for helping state and local governments target specific PWS and prioritize limited funding for infrastructure improvements. More extensive PWS service area boundary data will enable more accurate drinking water assessments in states where only estimated boundaries are currently available. Our statistical approach included the development of both categorical and continuous models rather than only considering MCL violations, as explored in prior work. Continuous models are important for protecting public health, because existing health-based thresholds (e.g., As and Pb) have declined over time with the availability of new health risk data and/or treatment options.63 Sensitivity analysis showed similar results at the 95th percentile, 75th percentile, and median drinking water concentrations (Table S2 and S3). Data from more PWS were above the detection threshold when the 95th percentile value was chosen (Table S2 and S3).

In this study, we analyzed a small subset of inorganic contaminants. We focused on four contaminants due to data availability, even though several hundred contaminants may be present in drinking water.64 Another study limitation included missing detection limits for datasets reported by state agencies. We assumed that the detection limit for each contaminant was the highest limit allowed by SDWA analytical methods (Table S5). Many drinking water datasets, including the one leveraged for this study, are highly censored. We addressed this issue by employing a hurdle model with two steps that included both categorical and continuous models. Much of the Mn data in this study were from the UCMR 3 database,21 which oversampled large PWS serving $greater than 10000$ individuals. Although some state data were included in our analysis for Mn (Table S1), results may be skewed toward large PWS. Data coverage by state varied from 41% to 95% of total PWS included in the database (Table S14). Although the number of PWS represented in the analysis varied among states, there were no discernable spatial patterns that would exclude specific subgroups (Table S14). The number of unique PWS available in the EWG dataset increased by 50% between 2005 and 2009 and was similar between 2009 and 2015 (Table S15). We assumed that PWS characteristics were constant over time because annual data were not available for 2005–2015. We used data on PWS characteristics available in SDWIS through the US EPA web-based API service.24 Accordingly, some characteristics may reflect PWS conditions outside of the studied time frame. A 2019 population density raster was used for dasymetric mapping, which falls outside the studied time frame. However, the US racial and ethnic makeup changed by $less than 2 percent$ between 2015 and 201965 and was similarly consistent between 2010 and 2020.66

Continuous models showed fewer statistically significant results than categorical models developed in this work, likely reflecting the limitations in the number and concentration ranges of detectable samples that restrict statistical power.67 We analyzed statistical associations at a higher spatial resolution than prior county scale analyses using direct PWS service areas provided by 16 state agencies. Estimated city/town boundaries were used for other areas and could be further resolved by additional state data in future work.15 Finally, US Census definitions for race and ethnicity in our analysis act as proxy measures for sociodemographic contexts in communities. Observed differences related to race and ethnicity vary due to societal differences, not biological or cultural differences.45 Despite the nation becoming increasingly multicultural, US Census categories have remained mostly unchanged, do not measure systemic structural racism due to discriminatory policies, and do not measure intersectionality. Drinking water contamination is a persistent problem across the United States for communities of all sizes and composition. Both federal and state policies are needed to ensure good quality, affordable water for everyone.68

#### Implications.

After accounting for variability due to environmental drivers (Excel Table S1), this study showed significant associations between the prevalence of limited English–speaking households served by PWS and higher detection and concentrations of regulated contaminants in drinking water. This result is supported by previous studies indicating that the deliberate exclusionary zoning of Hispanic communities (significantly correlated with linguistic isolation, Spearman’s $lowercase rho equals 0.65$ ) deprives these households of political power.52 In contrast, we found a lower probability of detecting As, Cr, and Se in PWS serving higher proportions of Black customers, but higher Cr, Mn, and Se concentrations among PWS with detectable concentrations, especially in nonmetropolitan areas. We did not find strong associations between poverty and drinking water contamination across the country. Finally, comparing analyses at two spatial units (PWS service area and county) allowed us to identify how aggregation bias can influence greater uncertainty in results at larger spatial units. Although effect sizes at the county scale were larger and less significant, these associations still indicated consistent directionality in comparison with the PWS service area scale. In the future, prioritizing data at local spatial resolutions will be crucial for understanding how to improve public drinking water systems to enhance equity for all people.
